subject: Connectivity choices for Private deployment (Peering vs PrivateLink vs S2S VPN)
messages:
From: Jordan Park <netops@asterhealth.com>
To: Lauren Bishop <lauren@redwoodinference.com>
Cc: Cloud Team <cloud-team@asterhealth.com>
Date: 2025-08-07T09:12:00-07:00
Subject: Connectivity options for Redwood Private deployment

Hi Lauren —

Thanks for the quick intro yesterday. As we scope the AsterHealth Private deployment (VPC in us-east-1, production on-prem DR in our Boston datacenter), our network team is evaluating three options to connect our traffic to Redwood inference endpoints:

- VPC Peering (direct peering between our VPC and Redwood's account VPC)
- AWS PrivateLink / interface endpoints (customers call back into Redwood over ENIs)
- Site-to-site IPsec VPN (encrypted tunnel from on-prem to Redwood VPC)

Primary concerns from our side:
- Source IP preservation (we need consistent client IPs for auditing and rate-limiting)
- Latency and egress cost (per-token egress billing sensitivity)
- Cross-region failover (ability to fail to us-west-2)
- Minimal operational overhead and easy troubleshooting for our NetOps team
- Compliance: SOC2 evidence of private connectivity and evidence to present to auditors

Can your team provide a short decision memo with: recommended primary option, fallback strategy, expected tradeoffs (latency, cost profile, visibility, complexity), and a mutual action plan (MAP) listing next steps and owners? If possible, include a simple diagram and a rough estimate of any incremental monthly cost for PrivateLink endpoints vs peering vs VPN.

We can do a 30-minute sync next week; available Tue/Wed mornings ET.

Thanks,
Jordan Park
NetOps Lead — AsterHealth

Jordan —

Appreciate the clear ask. Ben (SE) and Kimberly (Security) are looped for a technical breakdown and compliance perspective. Quick high-level thought before our call: PrivateLink tends to be the best fit when customers require an enforced VPC‑to‑service model with source-address masking protections and strong auditability, but it has per-endpoint costs and cross-region failover requires more orchestration. Peering gives lower latency and preserves native routing (source IP flow) but increases our attack surface and requires careful route/policy scoping. VPN is flexible and lowest-friction for on‑prem but usually has higher latency and is less predictable at scale.

Folks —

Following up with the tradeoff summary Jordan requested. I kept this pragmatic and focused on operational impact for AsterHealth's production workloads. Short version (recommendation after bullets below): Primary = AWS PrivateLink (interface endpoints) into a dedicated Redwood service VPC per region; Secondary / fallback = Site-to-site VPN for on‑prem DR and a restricted peering link for low-latency dev/test only.

Tradeoffs (Peering vs PrivateLink vs S2S VPN):

1) Connectivity model and security surface
   - VPC Peering: Full L3 routing between VPCs. Pros: low latency, no extra per‑connection cost. Cons: both VPCs can route to each other unless we tightly control route tables and security groups; cross-account peering requires route maintenance and does not provide an explicit service boundary. Source IPs preserved.
   - PrivateLink: Service model (our service exposed as ENIs in your VPC). Pros: Clear provider/customer separation, security boundary, easier to enforce least privilege. Cons: Per-interface-hour and per-GB data processing costs; by default source IP seen by Redwood is the endpoint ENI IP (we can pass through original client IP in headers at the application layer if desired).
   - Site-to-site VPN: Encrypted tunnel from your edge to our VPC. Pros: Quick to set up, works with on‑prem easily. Cons: Variable latency, throughput caps (depending on tunnel sizing), and typically added operational overhead to manage tunnels and BGP if used.

2) Source IP & auditing
   - Peering preserves source IP end-to-end (best for our audit log mapping).
   - PrivateLink masks source by default; we can add an X-Forwarded-For style header or use proxying patterns to capture the original IP for logs, but that requires app instrumentation and has security implications (header spoofing).
   - VPN preserves source IP for traffic originating from on‑prem; when used with NAT or internal proxies it can vary.

3) Cost profile (rough monthly estimates, ballpark):
   - Peering: minimal AWS network costs (inter-AZ/region depends), essentially zero per-hour resource cost on our side.
   - PrivateLink: ~ $0.01–0.05 per hour per endpoint (varies by region) + $0.01–$0.02 per GB processed. For steady production traffic expect incremental of several hundred to low-thousands USD/month depending on egress.
   - VPN: costs for managed VPN endpoints + data transfer; often cheaper on paper but can require bigger SRE effort.

4) Latency and failover
   - Peering: lowest latency within region. Cross-region failover requires separate peering or routing changes.
   - PrivateLink: low/medium latency; requires per-region endpoints. For cross-region failover we'll deploy endpoints in target region and route via customer-side control plane or DNS.
   - VPN: higher and more variable latency; good as DR but not ideal for tight tail latency SLOs.

5) Operational complexity and debugging
   - Peering: debugging is straightforward (route tables, SGs), but requires careful cross-account coordination.
   - PrivateLink: easier to reason about as a service; ENI endpoints are visible in your VPC; troubleshooting typically goes through both AWS ENI and our service logs.
   - VPN: requires tunnel monitoring, potential rekey events, and more frequent handoffs during maintenance windows.

Recommended approach (for AsterHealth, given your compliance and on‑prem DR requirements):
- Primary: PrivateLink per-region for production traffic. Rationale: clear security boundary, easier to present evidence to auditors, and we can instrument application headers to surface original client identity where needed.
- Secondary: Site-to-site VPN from Boston datacenter to Redwood service VPC in us-east-1 for DR and for workloads that must traverse on‑prem systems.
- Dev/Test: A narrowly scoped VPC Peering between dev VPCs for low-cost/low-latency experimentation.

Minimal MAP (draft):
- Redwood: prepare PrivateLink endpoint package (ARNs, required SG/route changes), provide recommended IAM role for endpoint creation — owner: Ben (action: send package) — due: 2025-08-09
- Aster: provision VPC endpoint subnet with /27 available, confirm routing policy and security group needs — owner: Jordan — due: 2025-08-12
- Redwood Security: produce short compliance artifact list for SOC2 (network diagrams, logging paths) — owner: Kimberly — due: 2025-08-11
- Joint: 30m pilot cutover and smoke test (create, test, validate) — target week of 8/18 — owners: Ben + Jordan

Attachments: redwood-aster-design-diagram.png (link above). I can run more precise cost numbers if you share expected baseline egress GB/day.

Regards,
Ben Carter
Senior Solutions Engineer — Redwood Inference

All — quick security/compliance notes and an ask for one small change to MAP.

Security notes:
- PrivateLink: strong isolation surface and easiest to document for SOC2. We should include a short appendix with: ENI ownership map, least-privilege SG template, expected CloudTrail events (ENI Create/Delete, Describe), and where flow logs will be retained.
- Source IP: Ben's suggestion to use application-layer X-Forwarded-For is acceptable but we must mark and validate the header at the app edge and include anti-spoof controls (only accept from Redwood internal ENI ranges). We'll provide a short integration checklist.
- Logs & retention: Aster will need evidence showing that access events for inference requests are captured for 12 months. We'll include examples of log records and a template auditor query.

MAP change request: add an explicit step for a short ATO-style checklist that Jordan's auditors can sign off on after the pilot. Proposal: after smoke test, we run a 2‑day verification window and produce the ATO checklist for your compliance team. Owner: Kimberly — due: 2025-08-22.

Jordan — if that works, we'll finalize the MAP and Ben will kick off the endpoint package. If you want, I can join the pilot call to walk auditors through the checklist.

Thanks,
Kimberly Park
Director, Security & Compliance — Redwood Inference
